fullPassage: Our brains are giant prediction machines, trying to figure out what will come next to us in the world. To do that, we need to extract patterns and commonalities, and create groupings of objects that are similar. We make sense of orchestras because we don't hear the 100 or so instruments as separate — our ears naturally group similar sounds together. All the violins automatically get merged in our head into a section (or two or three when they are playing different parts). Similarity can also apply to melodies as they are handed off from one instrument to another. Our brains apply certain rules that are inborn, to define similarity in several ways. An example is that notes that are close to one another in pitch space tend to get grouped together, and they separate — pop out — from other note clusters that are far apart from them. This is what allows us to hear a bass line as distinct from a guitar or clarinet line.

questions.passage: Our brains are giant prediction machines, trying to figure out what will come next to us in the world. To do that, we need to extract patterns and commonalities, and create groupings of objects that are similar. We make sense of orchestras because we don't hear the 100 or so instruments as separate — our ears naturally group similar sounds together. All the violins automatically get merged in our head into a section (or two or three when they are playing different parts). Similarity can also apply to melodies as they are handed off from one instrument to another. Our brains apply certain rules that are inborn, to define similarity in several ways. An example is that notes that are ____ to one another in pitch space tend to get grouped together, and they separate — pop out — from other note clusters that are far apart from them. This is what allows us to hear a bass line as distinct from a guitar or clarinet line.
